Authors: Alessandri, G., De Longis, E., & Doane, L. D.
Definition_ExactPhrase:
Abstract: “High emotional inertia, characterized by emotional states that carry over from one moment to the next” (page 1)

Introduction: “tendency of emotional states to be self-predictable over time and to be resistant to change, a condition called emotional inertia (Kuppens et al., 2010; Suls et al., 1998). Low levels of emotional inertia indicate higher tendency to change, while high levels indicate emotional states that persist from one moment to the next (Kuppens et al., 2010). Emotional inertia is usually measured by using the autocorrelation, or the autoregressive effect, of an emotion across time, which indicates the degree to which a current emotional state can be predicted by a previous emotional state and it is almost insensitive to the emotional level (Wang et al., 2012). Higher autocorrelations indicate more inert and self-predictive emotions, suggesting that any possible deviation from the mean is likely to persist for a long period of time. Conversely, low autocorrelations suggest low interdependency of repeated measures of an emotion, indicating that emotional states are relatively unpredictable over time (Wang et al., 2012).” (page 2)

In methods: "in accordance with our perspective, the estimated within-individual autoregressive coefficient represented a direct conceptualization of inertia as a trait-level, between-individual difference." (page 3)
Definition_ExactPhrase_LP:
the tendency of emotional states to be self-predictable over time and to be resistant to change (Page 2) 

emotional states that carry over from one moment to the next (Abstract)
Definition_Components: Carry over;Self-predicting;Resistance to change; inflexibility;Persisting; tendency to remain in same state;Slower recovery / return to baseline;Trait / person-level characteristic
Definition_Components_LP: Self-predicting;Resistance to change; inflexibility;Across contexts; spillover;
OperationalizeRecovery_How_ExactPhrase: "Higher autocorrelations indicate more inert and self-predictive emotions, suggesting that any possible deviation from the mean is likely to persist for a long period of time." (page 2)
